name: Pet First Aid Checklist
description: A checklist to help pet owners respond calmly to common emergencies and know when to call the veterinarian right away.

items.text: Save your vet and nearest emergency hospital numbers
Keep a pet poison helpline number handy
Stock and check a pet first aid kit
Know your pet's normal breathing and gum color
Keep a carrier or towel accessible at all times
items.note: Program emergency numbers into your phone in advance

items.text: Stay calm and keep yourself safe first
Approach slowly and speak in a soothing voice
Check if your pet is breathing and responsive
Look for bleeding, injuries, or distress
Call your vet to describe what you see
items.note: Use a towel or muzzle if a frightened pet may bite

items.text: Apply gentle, steady pressure with a clean cloth
Keep pressure on rather than peeking repeatedly
Cover the wound loosely once bleeding slows
Keep your pet calm and limit movement
Get to a vet for deep or heavy bleeding
items.note: Heavy or spurting bleeding is an emergency, so go at once

items.text: Look for pawing at the mouth or struggling to breathe
Open the mouth and remove a visible object if you can
Avoid pushing an object deeper into the throat
Keep airways clear and the pet as calm as possible
Rush to emergency care for ongoing breathing trouble
Note the substance and amount; keep the packaging
Do not induce vomiting unless a vet directs it
For overheating, move to shade and cool air
Offer small sips of water if your pet is alert
Call a vet or poison helpline immediately
items.note: Do not give human medicines to your pet

items.text: Support the body and avoid twisting an injured area
Use a carrier, board, or blanket as a stretcher
Keep your pet warm and calm during the trip
Call ahead so the clinic can prepare
Bring any packaging, medicines, or samples
This checklist is general information for owners, not veterinary advice; first aid does not replace professional care, so always consult a licensed veterinarian
items.note: In any emergency, contact your vet or an emergency animal hospital immediately

faq.q: When should I take my pet to an emergency vet?
faq.a: Seek emergency care for trouble breathing, severe bleeding, collapse, seizures, suspected poisoning, bloating, repeated vomiting, or major trauma. When in doubt, call your vet or an emergency animal hospital right away rather than waiting.

faq.q: How do I handle an injured pet safely?
faq.a: Even gentle pets may bite or scratch when hurt or scared. Move slowly, speak calmly, support the body, and use a towel or carrier. Protect yourself while you get your pet to care.

faq.q: What should I do if my pet may have been poisoned?
faq.a: Do not wait for symptoms. Note what and how much they may have taken, keep the packaging, and contact your veterinarian, an emergency hospital, or a pet poison helpline immediately for guidance.

faq.q: Can pet first aid replace seeing a vet?
faq.a: No. First aid is meant to stabilize your pet on the way to care, not to treat the problem. Always follow up with a veterinarian, even if your pet seems to recover.

faq.q: Is this pet first aid checklist printable?
faq.a: Yes. Print it or download the PDF, keep it with your emergency kit, and review it so the steps are familiar before you ever need them.
